The left hand takes the group of fingerholes nearest the mouthpiece and the right hand the group nearest the far end. It sounds with a brass-style mouthpiece: the lips buzz, and the shape of the mouth and the tightness of the lips adjust the pitch. It takes a lot of breath. Beginners first learn the six fingerholes in two groups, three per hand, then choose notes by opening and closing holes and by controlling the lips. Because the holes do not sit where acoustics would ideally put them, intonation is difficult, and the keys added later make it easier.
蛇形管號是文藝復興時期的低音管樂器，音色深沉、厚重且具有獨特的蒼涼感。其音質較為: The serpent is a Renaissance bass wind instrument with a deep, heavy timbre and a distinctive desolate quality. Its tone is dark and warm, carrying both the warmth of a woodwind and the solidity of a brass instrument, and its range lies mainly in the bass. Because the body is curved and pierced with many holes, it resonates in its own way and produces a natural, full-bodied sound. Compared with the bass reed pipes of the same period, the serpent's timbre is steadier and heavier; compared with the modern tuba or bassoon, its sound keeps more of an old, warm flavour and a slightly rough texture. That makes it particularly suited to the bass part in church music and in Renaissance polyphony.
蛇形管號琴身主要為木製，常見硬木如胡桃木、楓木、櫻桃木、梨木，亦有用楊木；外覆皮: The body of the serpent is mainly wood, usually a hardwood such as walnut, maple, cherry or pear, sometimes poplar, covered with leather or parchment. French makers glue together two halves cut in one continuous curve; English makers glue up several curved sections. A few are made of copper or brass, and may still be covered in leather. The mouthpiece was originally ivory, horn or hardwood, and the short pipe that takes the mouthpiece is brass. Modern copies use composite materials, polymers and 3D printing, and some have lightweight carbon-fibre bodies.

Repertoire you can hear includes Haydn's Divertimento in B-flat major for wind band, Mendelssohn's Calm Sea and Prosperous Voyage overture, the overture to his oratorio St. Paul, his Symphony No. 5, and Wagner's Rienzi overture. Today it appears in historically informed performance and in serpent ensembles.

In 1743 Lebeuf recorded that it was probably invented in 1590 by the Auxerre clergyman Guillaume, though direct evidence is limited. From the seventeenth century it was used in France to reinforce the cantus firmus and the bass part of plainchant, and it later passed into military bands, chamber music and orchestras. To improve intonation, keys were added from the end of the eighteenth century into the early nineteenth and an upright version appeared. In the middle and late nineteenth century it was gradually replaced by the ophicleide and the valved tuba; in the mid-twentieth century it was revived by historically informed performance, and modern makers have also improved it with new materials.

The serpent is an early lip-vibrated aerophone that developed in the Renaissance, Hornbostel–Sachs number 423.213. Its long, conical body is bent into a snake shape, mostly made of wood and covered with leather or parchment, fitted with a mouthpiece much like a trombone's and with six fingerholes, three for each hand. Players usually sit and hold the instrument upright between their knees, controlling pitch with lip vibration and by opening and closing the fingerholes. From the seventeenth century to the early nineteenth it was used to reinforce the bass part of church chant, and it also appeared in the bass parts of military music, chamber music and orchestras.
